chunks.text: She locked the door. He sat on the bed. The light was bad. She did not switch it on.
"Come here," she said.
He came. She undid his belt. The buckle clicked twice. His mouth tasted of gin. Her hands were cold.
She lay on her side. He lay on his. The fan turned. The light from the window was blue.
"You have something of mine," he said.
Karol drank his coffee. He set the cup down. He looked at the door.
He hit Karol once. The cup went off the table. It did not break. Karol went down. He sat on the floor and held his jaw.
He woke at six. The flat was cold. He stayed under the blanket. Outside, a tram on the wet street.

A note on the table. Two lines.

Going to Father. Back Sunday.

"She is here," her sister said.

"Good."

"She said do not come."

"All right."

He brought her to the bed under the high window where the rain was running silver down the panes and the lamps below in the courtyard threw a wandering amber against the ceiling, and she stood while he undressed her piece by piece as a man stripping the layers of some sacred and forbidden book, the lacework of her stays loosed and falling, the chemise lifted over the crown of her hair, the hem of her shift drawn away from the long pale arch of her flank.
After, he lay across her like a man fallen, and she held him there with her fingers in the wet of his hair, and the lamps in the courtyard guttered and the rain went on.

She came down the corridor with the candle held before her in her cupped hand and the wax running slow over her knuckles, and she found him in the long room where the curtains hung black and heavy as the vestments of some old order of mourning, and he turned at the sound of her step.
She would not afterward remember which of them had been the first to bring the other to the floor.

The morning came in slow upon the high window where the curtains hung half-drawn and the light fell across the bed in long stripes the colour of old gold, and she lay upon her side with her hair undone and her cheek against the bare hollow of his shoulder, and he was already half awake and watching the dust turn in the air.

He set his palm flat to the small of her back and held it there, and she felt the heat of him and she felt also the slow grief which had attended them both these last hours and had not gone away, only abated, only lain down with them in the dark and risen again in the morning beside them.

He turned and looked at her and she felt, for a moment, almost embarrassed, as if she had been caught at something, although there was nothing to catch her at; she had only been waiting for him. Or she had been waiting for him for half an hour and reading a book about, what, French art criticism, and trying not to listen for the buzzer. Both at once.

Later, on the bed, with the lamp off and the streetlight coming in cold across the duvet, she thought about how this had become familiar, how the shape of him over her was a shape she now knew, and she did not know what to do with knowing it. Was it a comfort or was it the slow shutting of a door. She did not know.

She put her hand in his hair and pulled, a little, the way he liked, and she heard him make a sound, and she thought, good. Then she thought, that is a strange thing to think. Then she stopped thinking, which was, she supposed, the point of it. For a while.
She had told him not to come. She had said it on the phone and again in the email, and she had thought, that is two times, that is enough, and then he came anyway.
She got up. They went into the kitchen because the kitchen was empty. She closed the door and then thought, why did I close the door.

She said, stop.

She was not sure she had said it. She said it again.

She woke up before the alarm, which surprised her — usually she slept right through it — and lay still for a while because moving would mean moving, would mean the day, would mean putting on the dressing gown which was on the back of the door and which she would have to cross the cold floor to reach, and instead she just lay there looking at the ceiling.

He had gone, she could tell, without listening for him, just by the quiet — the flat sounded the way it sounded when she was alone in it, which had a particular shape to it, a thinness, like a kettle that had stopped whistling. She did not mind. They had agreed about this.
0023. Hotel Continental, Room 814. Subject Two-One entered at 2358 with the asset; door secured 0001; ambient surveillance dark per protocol Black-Six.

Subsequent contact, eighteen minutes, conventional. Heart rate elevated, normal range for activity. No vocalisation above baseline. The mattress mechanism was silent. The wall to Room 813 was double-skinned and rated.

At 0019 the asset shifted. Two-One let her. She moved on top of him. Position maintained for nine minutes. Two-One disengaged at 0028, ten seconds before climax; the asset finished above, hand braced on his sternum, head turned away from the door.
0712. Warehouse 4, dock side, north bay. Pavlenko stood inside the rolling door with his hands visible. Reyes stood three paces inside the line, sidearm holstered, badge folded in the breast pocket.

"You are early," Pavlenko said.

"You are alone," Reyes said. "That is the wrong way around."
Pavlenko did not stop. Reyes drew, low ready, and the action took approximately one-point-two seconds from holster to muzzle on target. Pavlenko stopped.
She sat up. She wrapped the sheet around herself. The mark on her neck — left clavicle, approximately four centimetres lateral of the sternal notch — was faint. He noted it without comment.

"It was a mistake."

"Operationally?"

"Operationally."

"Yes."

"Personally also."

For three weeks she avoided him. She walked the long way to work, took the second elevator, ate lunch in the building across the street. By the time she stopped, she had forgotten why she had started.
They had been seeing each other for six months when she found the photograph. She did not ask about it for another year.
Anders spent the autumn in Berlin. He wrote letters that arrived once a fortnight. By December the letters had stopped, but she did not write to ask why.
She slept with him through the summer of '08, then through the year after, then into the slow grey of a third autumn. Her sister stopped asking who he was.
The first six months of their marriage she did not let him touch her in daylight. He did not press the matter. By the second winter the rule had quietly lapsed.
He had been with three women that year, in three cities, and each had ended the same way: the long silence between letters, then the letter that did not come.

In the months after the funeral she catalogued the apartment piece by piece. The clocks she gave to her cousins. The books she shipped to the library. The bed she could not bring herself to disassemble for two years.
By the time the cease-fire was announced he had been in the field for eleven months. He could not remember which of the four villages he had passed through was the one with the school.
She thought, I should go. She thought, but I will not. She thought several useless things in a small narrow row, the way she always did when the answer was already clear.
He stood at the window and tried to remember what he had been thinking when the train had stopped, the way you try to remember a dream that you know you have already lost.
She watched him sleep and did not know what she felt. Or she knew, in the way you know a thing by its weight on your chest, but she could not yet have given it a word.
The kitchen was painted yellow. There was a calendar on the wall from two years ago, still pinned to October. The refrigerator hummed. Sun came in over the back of the chair.
The room smelled of old smoke and lavender. A radiator ticked. The bedspread was wool, dark green, frayed at the corner where someone had picked at it.
Her body in the half-light was a long pale shape against the dark of the quilt. The mark of the strap had faded from her shoulder. The lamp on the table guttered.

"It is nothing," she said.

"It is not nothing."

"It is."

"You do not have to tell me what it is. But it is not nothing."

"Tell me what you want me to do," he said. His voice was lower than she remembered.

"You know what I want."

"Say it."
She put her hand on his chest to push him away and then did not push him away. They stood like that for a moment, her hand on his shirt. "Don't," she said, but she did not move her hand.

The kettle was boiling. She thought, this is the moment I should answer him. She thought, but the kettle. She took the kettle off the heat and the moment passed and neither of them said anything more.
He kicked the door. The lock held. He kicked it again. On the third kick the frame splintered and the door swung in on a dark room.
She struck him once across the face. The glass in her other hand did not spill. He did not raise a hand to his cheek; he just looked at her.
